# Cross-expert knowledge

1892 episode-level items from 71 kernels / 7 competitions; 602 rules supported by >= 2 kernels, covering 1449 items. Lever vocabulary: 40 categories.

## 1. build_full_pipeline_before_tuning  [L3]  —  15 kernels, 6 comps, 15 items

- **Context:** When starting a new competition notebook or converting a training notebook to inference, and no valid submission or leaderboard score exists yet, regardless of whether code is written from scratch, forked, or adapted from a training notebook.
- **Action:** Prioritize getting the complete end-to-end pipeline working (data loading → preprocessing → model loading/training → prediction → submission file writing) before tuning hyperparameters, augmentation, or model architecture. Remove dead/duplicated code, consolidate parameters into named constants, and submit once the pipeline completes to establish a baseline LB score, even if the score is expected to be poor. Only then make targeted changes one at a time to measure isolated effects.
- **Exceptions:** 53747598:e1#1 suggests deferring LB submission until all intended ensemble models are integrated, rather than submitting the first working single model. When bundling multiple changes early against a very weak baseline (49576186:e1#1), batching related changes in one submission may be acceptable since most changes are additive improvements.
- **Support:** kernels 13521245, 13542132, 27502740, 27656049, 27799930, 50496431, 52200959, 52551258, 52860091, 58130512, 59253662, 60759531, 6803050, 75145694, 77386286; comps amex-default-prediction, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Grandmaster': 4, 'Master': 4, 'Expert': 5, 'Contributor': 2}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 11, 'no': 4}
- **Cells:** L3/build/none_visible/part1, L3/build/none_visible/part2
- **Examples:**
  - `13521245:e1#1` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Grandmaster; steps 13521245:1->2, 13521245:3->4, 13521245:4->5): First build and verify the full inference pipeline (data loading, preprocessing, model loading, prediction, submission writing) with any available checkpoint, submit to confirm it works end-to-end, then swap in better checkpoints or change resolution. Do not tune augmentation or hyperparameters until the pipeline produces a valid submission.
  - `13542132:e1#2` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Master; steps 13542132:1->2, 13542132:2->3): Before tuning anything, consolidate all parameters into named constants, remove dead/duplicated code, wire up the full train-to-submission pipeline, and submit to get a baseline LB score. Only then make one targeted change at a time (e.g., one augmentation) and submit again to measure its isolated effect.
  - `27502740:e1#2` (amex-default-predict, Grandmaster; steps 27502740:1->2): Prioritize getting a complete train→predict→submit pipeline working and submitted before tuning the model. Fix infrastructure issues (memory, I/O) first, accept whatever baseline score results, then iterate on the modeling objective (loss, metric, features).
  - `27656049:e1#2` (amex-default-predict, Expert; steps 27656049:1->2, 27656049:2->3, 27656049:3->4, 27656049:4->5): Build the pipeline in stages: first data loading and exploration, then minimal training, then inference and submission generation. Fix bugs and add instrumentation (timing, memory) before scaling up model complexity. Only submit to the leaderboard once the full pipeline runs end-to-end and produces reasonable validation metrics. Withhold submission until you switch to cross-validation for a robust estimate.

Only after the pipeline runs end-to-end, begin tuning hyperparameters. Do not tune before you can evaluate.

Submit only after the full pipeline executes without errors. Do not attempt model or hyperparameter changes until a baseline score is obtained.

## 2. stop_sweep_after_budget_exhausted  [L3]  —  11 kernels, 6 comps, 11 items

- **Context:** You have tried 3-5+ meaningfully different configurations of a single lever (blend weights, feature variants, hyperparameter values) without any variant matching or exceeding the baseline on the leaderboard, or consecutive attempts produce score changes smaller than ~0.1-0.2% of the metric with no monotonic improvement trend.
- **Action:** Abandon the current lever and move to a structurally different approach (new features, new model architecture, different ensemble strategy). Do not keep micro-tuning within the same narrow parameter range. Limit fine-grained sweeps of secondary parameters to 3-5 submissions before pivoting. Lock the parameter at the best-known value.
- **Exceptions:** If the lever was only partially applied or a bug was present, complete the intended modification before abandoning (55591012:e14#2).
- **Support:** kernels 15082684, 17616127, 18851026, 27389424, 27836972, 50376011, 53762022, 55987255, 58130512, 73937748, 77276039; comps amex-default-prediction, commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Master': 5, 'Contributor': 2, 'Grandmaster': 2, 'Expert': 2}; episode reached new best: {'no': 7, 'yes': 4}
- **Cells:** L3/sweep/new_idea/part3, L3/sweep/new_idea/part4
- **Examples:**
  - `15082684:e2#1` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Master; steps 15082684:3->4, 15082684:4->5, 15082684:5->6, 15082684:6->7): Submit a handful of checkpoints spanning different training runs and epochs. If none beat the current best after ~5-6 tries and the CV-to-LB correlation appears weak (high CV doesn't yield high LB), stop the sweep and change approach rather than exhaustively testing all checkpoints. Track the best LB explicitly and revert to it before moving on.
  - `17616127:e35#1` (commonlitreadability, Contributor; steps 17616127:122->123, 17616127:123->124, 17616127:124->125): When incremental weight changes stop improving score, try a radical pruning experiment (remove most members, keep only the strongest subset). If it causes a large regression, immediately revert and conclude the current member set is near-optimal. Then switch to a qualitatively different lever (new features, new model architectures) rather than continuing to micro-tune weights.
  - `18851026:e1#2` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18851026:2->3, 18851026:3->4): After testing a few discrete options on a secondary lever, if the best gain is small and a variant regresses substantially, stop the sweep and pivot to a higher-impact lever (e.g., richer features, additional base models, or a fundamentally different blending strategy) rather than continuing to tune the same lever.
  - `27389424:e17#3` (amex-default-predict, Grandmaster; steps 27389424:131->132, 27389424:132->133, 27389424:133->134): Set a budget (e.g., 10-15 trials) for any single hyperparameter sweep. If no clear optimum is found, lock the parameter at the best-known value and move to a different lever. Avoid combining multiple lever changes in one step, as it confounds the signal.
  - `27836972:e9#2` (amex-default-predict, Expert; steps 27836972:48->49, 27836972:54->55): After exploring 3-4 meaningfully different configurations of a feature idea without any variant matching or exceeding the baseline on both CV and LB, abandon the idea and move to a structurally different feature engineering approach. Do not keep micro-tuning which columns to include.
  - `50376011:e8#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50376011:29->30, 50376011:30->31): After exhausting the discrete options, stop the sweep and pivot to a qualitatively different approach rather than re-combining the same elements. The best single-group result serves as the baseline for the next lever.

## 3. add_architecturally_diverse_backbone_to_ensemble  [L2]  —  11 kernels, 3 comps, 12 items

- **Context:** When an ensemble of models from a single architecture family (e.g., all 2D CNNs, all GBDTs of one type, all RoBERTa) has plateaued and checkpoint/hyperparameter/weight-tuning sweeps yield diminishing returns.
- **Action:** Introduce a model from a fundamentally different architecture family (e.g., transformer-based vs CNN-based, DeBERTa when existing are RoBERTa, CatBoost vs LightGBM, CNN on reshaped tabular data vs MLP). Validate the new architecture produces reasonable standalone predictions first, then blend with existing members using a conservative weight for the new member. Submit after each addition to confirm monotonic improvement. If the new backbone doesn't help after 2-3 weight adjustments, remove it before trying others.
- **Exceptions:** Not every new backbone improves the score — NextViT-large regressed in 49524919:e26. The new architecture must be genuinely complementary, not just different. Same-family additions (e.g., CatBoost added to LightGBM, Funnel-large when you already have RoBERTa) may provide minimal diversity gain (55431616:e3#2, 18550705). Late-stage additions of same-family variants with different target transforms yield diminishing returns (73937748:e24#2).
- **Support:** kernels 18423958, 18523075, 18550705, 18837555, 18851026, 49524919, 50496431, 52860091, 73671444, 73937748, 75145694; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Master': 4, 'Expert': 3, 'Grandmaster': 5}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 12}
- **Cells:** L2/ensemble_composition/part2
- **Examples:**
  - `18423958:e5#2` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18423958:12->13): Combine at least 2-3 architecturally diverse transformer backbones (e.g., encoder-only, encoder-decoder, distilled) with fold-averaged predictions per backbone. Weight stronger standalone models more heavily (e.g., 0.6) and weaker ones less (0.4). Adding a third diverse model often beats a two-model blend even if the third model is individually weaker.
  - `18523075:e2#1` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18523075:3->4, 18523075:4->5): Replace the weakest existing backbone with a stronger one from a different architecture family first (one swap at a time), submit to verify improvement, then add a completely new architecture as an additional member. Flatten ensemble weights toward uniform when adding diverse models rather than heavily favoring any single model. Submit after each backbone change to confirm the direction.
  - `18550705:e3#1` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18550705:9->10): Prefer adding backbones with fundamentally different attention mechanisms (e.g., DeBERTa's disentangled attention vs. standard transformers) rather than variants of existing architectures. Pair the new backbone with a proven model head design (attention pooling, multisample dropout) already validated on other members. If the addition improves the score, keep it; if not, remove it promptly as was done with Funnel/BART.
  - `18837555:e3#2` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18837555:10->11, 18837555:11->12): Introduce a model variant that pools differently—e.g., concatenate the last N hidden layers instead of using only the final layer, combine CLS token representation with attention-weighted pooling. This increases prediction diversity within the same backbone family, improving ensemble gains without requiring a different pretrained model.
  - `18851026:e4#1` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18851026:9->10): Integrate a pretrained model from a different architecture family (e.g., T5 when you already have RoBERTa). Extract embeddings using the same stacking pipeline (SVR/Ridge on embeddings), then blend with existing predictions. Start with a high weight on the new component to test its contribution, then adjust.
  - `49524919:e18#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 49524919:72->73, 49524919:73->74, 49524919:75->76): Add a structurally different backbone (e.g., transformer-based vs CNN-based) as a new ensemble member. First upgrade the existing backbone to a larger variant to confirm capacity helps, then add the new architecture, then blend with equal weights. Submit after each addition to confirm monotonic improvement. If each addition improves, continue adding more diverse architectures.

## 4. isolate_one_change_per_submission  [L3]  —  10 kernels, 5 comps, 13 items

- **Context:** When you have 2+ independent levers to test (e.g., new features, preprocessing, hyperparameters, ensemble members, model swaps) and leaderboard submissions or evaluation cycles are the primary evaluation signal.
- **Action:** Change at most one conceptually distinct variable per submission or evaluation cycle. Fix all other variables and submit to isolate the effect. If you bundle multiple changes and get a regression, you cannot attribute it and must waste iterations unwinding. Only after each lever's marginal value is known should you combine them. Hold the model checkpoint fixed when testing preprocessing changes, or submit the checkpoint-only change first before layering preprocessing changes on top. Limit to 2-3 unsubmitted versions before getting evaluation feedback.
- **Exceptions:** When levers are inherently coupled (e.g., a checkpoint was trained with specific preprocessing), joint changes may be unavoidable. Also, when reverting a known-bad change, bundling the revert with a new change can work (7676170:e3#1 v17). When local validation is cheap and you plan an add-then-prune strategy with many candidate features, adding all at once then pruning can be faster (27799930:e4#1).
- **Support:** kernels 27799930, 27836972, 49524919, 49576186, 50496431, 52860091, 58130512, 7018718, 7676170, 77276039; comps amex-default-prediction, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate; tiers {'Contributor': 2, 'Expert': 7, 'Grandmaster': 3, 'Master': 1}; episode reached new best: {'no': 11, 'yes': 2}
- **Cells:** L3/consolidate/plateau, L3/explore/new_idea/part1, L3/explore/new_idea/part2
- **Examples:**
  - `27799930:e5#3` (amex-default-predict, Contributor; steps 27799930:36->37): Submit or validate after each conceptually distinct change (e.g., adding date features vs. adding lag features). When multiple changes are bundled and the result regresses, you cannot tell which change caused the regression. Limit to 2-3 untested versions before getting evaluation feedback.
  - `27836972:e8#2` (amex-default-predict, Expert; steps 27836972:36->37, 27836972:37->38, 27836972:38->39, 27836972:39->40): Add one feature group at a time, record CV. If CV improves, keep it and add the next idea. If CV drops, comment out or remove that feature before proceeding. Only submit to LB when CV shows clear improvement over the prior best. If two consecutive LB submissions fail to beat the best, consider the feature direction exhausted and pivot to a different approach.
  - `49524919:e13#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 49524919:53->54): Before introducing a second model into an ensemble, clean up the existing pipeline: parameterize hard-coded values into config, remove dead code for abandoned approaches, and verify the single-model baseline is solid. This reduces debugging surface when stacking models and ensures config-driven reproducibility.
  - `49576186:e18#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 49576186:101->102, 49576186:102->103, 49576186:103->104, 49576186:104->105): When testing preprocessing changes, try to hold the model checkpoint fixed, or at minimum submit the checkpoint-only change first (as in v102→v103) before layering preprocessing changes on top. If a bundled change regresses, do a broader cleanup rather than trying to revert individual pieces.
  - `49576186:e19#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 49576186:109->110, 49576186:112->113): Test single-modality ablation on the leaderboard before committing. If the score regresses substantially (e.g., >5% relative), immediately revert to multi-modality. Do not bundle modality ablation with other large changes (augmentation, sampling) — isolate the modality change to get a clean signal.
  - `49576186:e22#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 49576186:131->132, 49576186:132->133, 49576186:133->134, 49576186:134->135): Test the new architecture with all modalities first to isolate the architecture effect. Then systematically remove modalities one at a time (keeping the rest fixed) to find the best subset. If all variants score worse than the pre-change baseline, revert the architectural change and stop the ablation. Do not combine multiple untested changes (new architecture + modality removal) without first validating each independently.

## 5. defer_submission_until_pipeline_runs_cleanly  [L2]  —  9 kernels, 5 comps, 10 items

- **Context:** When building or modifying an inference/feature pipeline that has multiple integration points (model loading, data processing, column alignment) and runtime errors are likely.
- **Action:** Do not submit to the leaderboard until the pipeline runs end-to-end without errors. Fix bugs iteratively across multiple notebook versions, inspecting outputs (shapes, head, distributions) after each fix. Only submit once all components produce valid output. This conserves submission budget and avoids interpreting scores from broken pipelines.

## 6. revert_first_on_large_regression  [L3]  —  8 kernels, 6 comps, 10 items

- **Context:** When a change (especially a compound one) causes a score regression relative to the previous best, and you have a clear record of which configuration produced that best score.
- **Action:** Immediately revert all changes to the last known-good full configuration (ensemble membership, weights, settings) rather than trying to fix the regression by tuning other hyperparameters on top. Confirm the baseline score is restored. For large regressions (>~10-15% relative), revert within 1-2 iterations—do not persist for more than one follow-up attempt. Then re-introduce changes one at a time to test if a variation improves on the restored baseline. If a multi-change version regressed, isolate by reverting the suspected harmful change while restoring the suspected beneficial setting. After reverting, try a smaller variation of the same idea if desired.
- **Exceptions:** If the regression is tiny (e.g., <0.0001) and CV improved, the drop may be noise—consider a complementary fix rather than full revert (75145694:e16#1). When the regression is small (<0.2% absolute) and you have high-confidence orthogonal improvements queued, layering additional changes may be viable (27799930:e8#2). When you believe the approach is architecturally correct and the regression is from integration bugs, debug first before reverting (49524919:e26#2).
- **Support:** kernels 15372370, 17616127, 49576186, 50496431, 52860091, 58130512, 7676170, 77450317; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Expert': 2, 'Contributor': 2, 'Grandmaster': 4, 'Master': 2}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 7, 'no': 3}
- **Cells:** L3/consolidate/regression, L3/explore/new_idea/part1, L3/explore/new_idea/part2
- **Examples:**
  - `15372370:e5#1` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Expert; steps 15372370:9->10, 15372370:10->11): Revert the changes incrementally rather than all at once: remove the most aggressive/novel component first, test, then remove remaining novel components. This isolates which change caused the regression. If the score still hasn't recovered after partial revert, continue removing until you return to baseline behavior.
  - `17616127:e33#1` (commonlitreadability, Contributor; steps 17616127:115->116, 17616127:116->117): Revert to the full ensemble membership that produced your best score, re-enable all model/fold predictions that were active at that time, then make one targeted swap of a blend component to test if a slight variation improves on the restored baseline. Do the restoration as a preparatory step without submitting, then submit only after the final adjustment.
  - `49576186:e21#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 49576186:129->130, 49576186:130->131): Revert the most complex/novel components (e.g., elaborate sampling logic) back to the simpler baseline version, but retain the smaller, well-understood additions (e.g., label smoothing, mixed precision). This avoids losing all progress while removing the likely culprit. Submit the simplified version to confirm recovery before trying new directions.
  - `50496431:e34#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:113->114, 50496431:116->117, 50496431:118->119): Revert the regression-causing change within 1-2 iterations. If the change was compound (architecture + reshape + ensemble), decompose it: keep the parts most likely correct and revert the rest. Do not persist with a large regression for more than one follow-up attempt. After reverting, try a smaller variation of the same idea.
  - `50496431:e35#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:124->125): Revert most changes back to the last known-good configuration in a single step, then selectively re-enable components one at a time. Prioritize reverting preprocessing and augmentation changes first since they affect all ensemble members. Submit after each revert to confirm recovery before adding new changes.
  - `52860091:e8#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 52860091:29->30, 52860091:33->34, 52860091:37->38, 52860091:40->41): When adding a new model to an ensemble causes a surprising regression, first revert to the known-good baseline to confirm it still works. Then re-enable the new member after checking for config/data issues (re-runs, log inspection). Only after confirming the new member runs correctly should you evaluate its contribution. Test the new member in isolation to establish its standalone quality before blending.

## 7. isolate_one_variable_per_submission  [L3]  —  8 kernels, 4 comps, 12 items

- **Context:** When testing multiple independent changes (e.g., preprocessing + model hyperparameter, feature + architecture, or infrastructure + experimental change) and each could independently cause a regression, especially near a personal best score where you want to attribute any score change to a specific change.
- **Action:** Change only one lever per submission so regressions or improvements can be attributed. Separate infrastructure changes from experimental changes: submit infrastructure-only first to confirm parity, then layer the experiment. If you bundled multiple changes and regressed, partially revert the most suspicious change first or bisect to isolate the cause. If two consecutive bundled submissions regress, revert fully before trying something else. Do not continue stacking on a regressed state—unbundle.
- **Exceptions:** When all pending changes are independently low-risk (e.g., bug fixes + infrastructure), bundling is acceptable to conserve submission budget (77450317:e8#2). When local CV is reliable and changes are minor, bundling for local evaluation is fine (60197293:e9#2). When you have high confidence that multiple changes are each independently correct (e.g., matching known training settings) and submission budget is limited, bundling is acceptable (15082684:e4#2, 59253662:e3#2).
- **Support:** kernels 17371717, 27656049, 28093671, 50496431, 53762022, 58130512, 59253662, 60197293; comps amex-default-prediction, commonlitreadabilityprize, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate; tiers {'Master': 4, 'Expert': 2, 'Contributor': 4, 'Grandmaster': 2}; episode reached new best: {'no': 12}
- **Cells:** L3/probe/new_idea/part2, L3/probe/new_idea/part3
- **Examples:**
  - `17371717:e8#1` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 17371717:17->18): Keep the new technique in place and swap only the suspected factor (e.g., checkpoint source). If the score partially recovers, the technique is likely sound but needs the right supporting configuration. If it doesn't recover, revert the technique itself next.
  - `27656049:e5#1` (amex-default-predict, Expert; steps 27656049:16->17, 27656049:17->18): When probing a new idea, change only one lever per submission so regressions can be attributed. If you bundle changes and regress, partially revert the most suspicious change first. If two consecutive submissions both regress from the baseline, abandon the new ideas and revert fully before trying something else.
  - `28093671:e10#2` (amex-default-predict, Contributor; steps 28093671:41->42): First revert cleanly to the last-best configuration and confirm the score is restored. Only then layer on new changes (hyperparameter tuning, regularization) in a separate submission. Bundling revert + new changes makes it impossible to diagnose whether the new changes help or hurt relative to the true baseline.
  - `50496431:e15#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:45->46): Keep the confirmed-beneficial change active and add only the new change in the next submission. If you instead revert the beneficial change while adding the new one, a regression tells you nothing about which change caused it. Always change one variable per submission when probing.
  - `50496431:e19#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:58->59, 50496431:59->60): When probing multiple independent changes, if the first regresses, revert it before testing the second. Stacking a new change on a regressed baseline confounds signals—you cannot tell if the second change helps or hurts. Always return to the best-known baseline between independent probes.
  - `53762022:e2#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Contributor; steps 53762022:5->6, 53762022:6->7): When substituting a new checkpoint, first submit with the original hyperparameters to isolate the checkpoint effect. Only after confirming the checkpoint works, change one hyperparameter at a time. Never change both checkpoint and architecture hyperparameters without intermediate validation, as a regression becomes undiagnosable.

## 8. staged_build_defer_submission  [L3]  —  8 kernels, 4 comps, 8 items

- **Context:** When a major pipeline change (new model framework, new feature source, multi-step refactor) spans multiple code edits and intermediate states are incomplete or buggy, or when making multiple related infrastructure and hyperparameter changes (more folds, patience, code restructuring) from a working baseline where each intermediate state may not be submittable.
- **Action:** Build in stages without submitting: implement, debug imports/paths/shapes, and verify end-to-end execution across 2-5 unsubmitted iterations, verifying locally via CV logs or execution output. Only submit once the full pipeline produces valid output and runs cleanly end-to-end. If an environment error blocks submission, fix it minimally and submit that version. This conserves submission quota and avoids misleading partial scores.
- **Exceptions:** none

## 9. stop_sweep_after_consecutive_regressions  [L3]  —  8 kernels, 4 comps, 8 items

- **Context:** 3-4 consecutive submissions tuning the same lever (e.g., augmentation, hyperparameters, preprocessing, checkpoint variants) all score below the established best, with no improving trend.
- **Action:** Stop the sweep on that lever. Revert to the last-known-best configuration and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., architecture, loss function, ensembling, new model family). Do not continue making small perturbations to the same set of parameters.
- **Exceptions:** If scores are trending upward within the sweep (58130512:e37#3: 0.81999→0.82240), one more attempt may be warranted. Some authors use a threshold of 4-5 rather than 3 (13542132:e3#1: continued one extra step).

## 10. revert_regressing_change_before_iterating  [L3]  —  7 kernels, 6 comps, 7 items

- **Context:** A recent change (feature selection method, preprocessing step, post-processing branch, configuration change, or ensemble member swap) caused a leaderboard regression confirmed across one or more consecutive submissions, especially when two or more consecutive submissions regress from a known-good configuration.
- **Action:** Revert the suspected regressing change entirely and restore the exact last-known-good state. Submit to confirm recovery before making any additional modifications. Do not combine the revert with new untested changes (hyperparameter tweaks, data reordering, new features) in the same submission, as this confounds diagnosis and risks compounding regressions. ## 13. one_variable_at_a_time  [L3]  —  7 kernels, 4 comps, 7 items

- **Context:** You are tuning hyperparameters or configuration knobs near a plateau and need to attribute gains or losses to specific changes.
- **Action:** Change only one knob per submission so you can attribute the result. If you changed multiple knobs simultaneously and regressed, revert to the last-known-good configuration, then vary only one parameter per subsequent submission. Avoid confounded results that waste submissions.
- **Exceptions:** When two settings are inherently coupled (e.g., feature-selection file must match the model ensemble), they must be changed together (58130512:e37#1). Authors frequently violate this rule in practice (58130512:e30#1, 55621328:e17#2).

## 14. isolate_regression_cause_by_sequential_revert  [L3]  —  6 kernels, 5 comps, 7 items

- **Context:** A bundle of changes (e.g., data change + architecture change, or window size + ensemble composition + blending method) caused a score regression, and you need to identify which factor hurt.
- **Action:** Revert all changes back to the last-known-good configuration. Then re-apply changes one at a time, starting with the most likely beneficial change or reverting factors one at a time starting with the most suspicious. ## 16. incremental_debugging_without_submission  [L3]  —  6 kernels, 4 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When a large code refactor, data source change, or new feature addition introduces runtime errors, import failures, or variable mismatches and the error source is unclear.
- **Action:** Make small targeted fixes across successive saves/versions without submitting to the leaderboard. Run cell-by-cell: fix stale debug code, then broken paths, then stale caches, then API/import issues. Only submit once the pipeline executes cleanly end-to-end. Budget 2-5 micro-fix iterations for a major structural change. This conserves submission budget and avoids confounding bug fixes with feature impact assessment.

## 17. change_one_variable_at_a_time  [L3]  —  6 kernels, 4 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When probing whether a new configuration (model variant, architecture, hyperparameter) improves over a strong baseline, and multiple changes are tempting to bundle together.
- **Action:** Change only one variable at a time against the baseline. If you must bundle tightly coupled changes, accept that a regression won't tell you which change caused it. After a clear regression from bundled changes, revert all changes entirely rather than trying to compensate with minor tweaks. Re-test components individually only if the idea still seems promising.
- **Exceptions:** When changes are logically inseparable (e.g., new checkpoint requires matching preprocessing), bundling is acceptable per 55621328:e48#1, but revert the entire bundle on regression.
- **Support:** kernels 13848868, 28984551, 55621328, 58130512, 59253662, 6803050; comps amex-default-prediction, google-quest-challenge, learning-agency-lab-automate, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Grandmaster': 1, 'Contributor': 2, 'Master': 3}; episode reached new best: {'no': 6}
- **Cells:** L3/probe/new_idea/part5
- **Examples:**
  - `13848868:e3#1` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Grandmaster; steps 13848868:10->11, 13848868:11->12): Change only one variable at a time against the baseline. If you must bundle changes, be prepared that a regression won't tell you which change caused it, forcing additional experiments to disentangle. After a clear regression, revert all changes rather than toggling minor post-processing flags, which cannot compensate for a large drop from core model changes.
  - `28984551:e2#1` (amex-default-predict, Contributor; steps 28984551:2->3): Change only one thing at a time when probing a new algorithm variant. If you must change two settings (e.g., boosting type and learning rate), first test the variant with all other hyperparameters held constant so you can attribute any score change to the variant itself. If the probe causes a large regression (>1% relative), abandon it immediately rather than tuning around it, and move to a structurally different approach.
  - `55621328:e48#1` (learning-agency-lab-, Master; steps 55621328:142->143, 55621328:143->144, 55621328:144->145): Bundle tightly coupled infrastructure changes (model swap, preprocessing toggle, device handling) into a single submission rather than submitting each independently. But if the bundle scores poorly, you cannot isolate which change caused the regression — so revert to the last known-good configuration and re-test components individually rather than continuing to tweak within the failed bundle.
  - `58130512:e8#2` (learning-agency-lab-, Master; steps 58130512:22->23): When reverting a failed probe, make only the revert and submit to confirm the baseline is restored. Bundle unrelated changes into a separate commit afterward. Mixing revert with other changes makes it impossible to diagnose whether the revert worked or the other changes caused a new problem.
  - `59253662:e6#1` (learning-agency-lab-, Contributor; steps 59253662:26->27, 59253662:28->29): Treat adding a new stacking member as a single probe: integrate it in one change, submit, and compare against baseline. If the leaderboard score regresses or fails to improve, abandon the idea quickly rather than tuning integration details. A small regression suggests the new predictions add noise or redundancy rather than complementary signal.
  - `6803050:e15#1` (google-quest-challen, Master; steps 6803050:60->61): Change only one variable at a time when probing. If you revert component A and simultaneously disable component B, a regression tells you nothing about which mattered. Instead, revert one, submit, then revert the other separately. This costs one extra submission but gives clean signal.

## 18. staged_multi_component_integration  [L3]  —  6 kernels, 3 comps, 11 items

- **Context:** When adding a new model architecture or multiple new components (new backbone, restructured fusion, new weights) to an existing multi-model inference pipeline, especially when the new component requires changes to preprocessing, loading, or aggregation logic and components depend on each other for full benefit.
- **Action:** First add the new model code/weights and verify standalone predictions (use strict checkpoint loading to surface mismatches). Then fix preprocessing/TTA/loading issues across 1-2 iterations. Finally re-enable existing ensemble members and tune blend weights. Build across 2-3 versions without expecting score improvement at each step; tolerate intermediate regressions and evaluate only after full integration is complete. Do not judge the new model's value until it is properly integrated alongside existing members. If the final combined score doesn't beat the baseline, revert.
- **Exceptions:** 50496431:e30#1 — the final score didn't beat the prior best, and the author reverted, suggesting this strategy doesn't always pay off. 50496431:e33#1 suggests an A/B/AB pattern as an alternative when the new model is already properly loading. 50496431:e10#1 notes the intermediate regression was significant and persisted for two versions, so each step must be verified carefully.
- **Support:** kernels 49524919, 50496431, 52200959, 55431616, 55987255, 7548275; comps google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate; tiers {'Grandmaster': 8, 'Master': 2, 'Expert': 1}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 4, 'no': 7}
- **Cells:** L3/build/new_idea/part1, L3/build/new_idea/part2, L3/build/new_idea/part3
- **Examples:**

Then submit a minimal cleanup version to confirm the pipeline works end-to-end. Only then change the blending/submission logic in a separate step. This isolates bugs: if the score regresses, you know it's the blend weights, not the plumbing.
  - `49524919:e30#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 49524919:136->137, 49524919:137->138, 49524919:138->139): First, add the new model and its infrastructure while disabling (via 'continue') existing model loops, and submit to verify the new model runs correctly and produces reasonable standalone predictions. Then add a second backbone variant to the same group and test it similarly. Finally, remove all skip statements, include the new group in the blend with rebalanced weights, and submit the full ensemble. Expect intermediate regressions; treat them as diagnostics, not failures.
  - `50496431:e10#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:29->30, 50496431:30->31): First submit a version that removes the old inline feature generation and simplifies the pipeline (accept a temporary score regression). Tolerate intermediate regressions and evaluate only after the full integration is complete. If the final combined score doesn't beat the baseline, revert the ensemble composition rather than the individual models.

Periodically re-run even unchanged code to detect upstream artifact updates.

## 21. prune_weak_ensemble_members  [L2]  —  6 kernels, 3 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When an ensemble member has noticeably worse standalone/OOF scores than other members, or when adding a new member causes a score regression.
- **Action:** Remove the weakest or newly-regressing member entirely rather than relying on weight optimization to suppress it. Re-evaluate the ensemble after each removal. Even with optimized blend weights, a weak or redundant member can hurt because the optimizer may overfit to its noise. If removal improves the score, continue pruning the next weakest member.
- **Exceptions:** In larger ensembles with many diverse architectures, even weaker members can help through diversity (18757376 notes this). Also, when the number of base models is very small (≤5), removing members may increase variance more than it reduces bias (7573212:e4#2).
- **Support:** kernels 18550705, 18757376, 18851026, 50376011, 50496431, 7548275; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Master': 2, 'Expert': 2, 'Grandmaster': 2}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 3, 'no': 3}
- **Cells:** L2/ensemble_composition/part1
- **Examples:**
  - `18550705:e2#2` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18550705:6->7, 18550705:7->8, 18550705:8->9): Remove the model you have least confidence in first (e.g., the one with the most different architecture or worst standalone CV). Submit after each removal. If score improves, continue pruning the next weakest. If score worsens, restore that member and try removing a different one instead.
  - `18757376:e4#2` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18757376:5->6): In a transformer stacking ensemble, compare OOF RMSE of each backbone group. If a weaker backbone group degrades the blend, remove it entirely rather than downweighting it. Fewer but stronger members often outperform more diverse but noisier ones on small datasets.
  - `18851026:e6#3` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18851026:19->20): If adding diverse models to a blend doesn't improve over the previous best after fixing integration issues, try removing the weakest or most correlated member and rebalancing weights rather than continuing to add more members.
  - `50376011:e3#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50376011:8->9, 50376011:9->10, 50376011:10->11): If adding a checkpoint to an averaging ensemble worsens the leaderboard score, that checkpoint is likely weaker or too correlated with existing members. Remove it and do not include it in further combinations. More members is not always better; prefer a smaller, higher-quality set.
  - `50496431:e53#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:210->211, 50496431:211->212): First test the new backbone as a swap for an existing member (not an addition) to isolate its contribution. If it does not improve or match the member it replaces, remove it and restore the previous member before trying other changes. Do not keep a new backbone that adds no measurable gain.
  - `7548275:e5#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7548275:19->20): Remove the weakest model from the ensemble entirely (don't just rely on the optimizer to zero its weight). Re-run and check LB. Even with weight optimization, removing a bad model can yield large gains because the optimizer may not fully suppress it across all targets/folds.

## 22. maximize_architectural_diversity_across_axes  [L2]  —  6 kernels, 2 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When the ensemble is dominated by one model family, one pooling strategy, or one input representation, and you want to reduce ensemble correlation.
- **Action:** Add models that differ from existing members on at least two axes: backbone architecture (e.g., CNN vs ViT vs pure convolution), input format (e.g., spectrograms vs raw signals vs different resolutions), and head/pooling strategy (e.g., attention pooling vs mean pooling vs multi-layer concat). Test each new model solo first, then add to the blend. Even individually weaker models can improve the ensemble if they capture complementary patterns.
- **Exceptions:** 18837555:e2#1 showed slight regression when adding a multi-layer attention model, suggesting diversity alone doesn't guarantee improvement—the new member must be reasonably strong.
- **Support:** kernels 18426209, 18550705, 18837555, 49524919, 52200959, 53747598; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Expert': 2, 'Master': 3, 'Grandmaster': 1}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 5, 'no': 1}
- **Cells:** L2/ensemble_composition/part3
- **Examples:**
  - `18426209:e3#2` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18426209:4->5): Add a new model that uses a structurally different pooling method (e.g., mean pooling + layer norm vs attention pooling) over the same or different backbone. Load fold-averaged predictions from that model and blend with existing predictions. Start with equal weights and tune from there.
  - `18550705:e1#1` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18550705:1->2): Add models from different transformer families (different pretraining objectives) and simultaneously upgrade pooling from single-token output to concatenated mean+max over weighted hidden layers with attention pooling. Double the linear head input dimension to match the concatenated representation. Test as a single probe submission to validate the direction before expanding further.
  - `18837555:e2#1` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18837555:6->7): Add a model variant that differs in its pooling mechanism (e.g., multi-layer concatenation + attention head vs. single-layer attention). Load its checkpoints, generate predictions, and include them in a simple uniform average. Submit to check for improvement; if the score is flat or slightly worse, continue adding more diverse sources before concluding the approach failed.
  - `49524919:e20#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 49524919:88->89, 49524919:89->90): Add one new architecturally distinct backbone at a time. First submit the new model solo to gauge its standalone quality. Then enable it in the full blend with approximately equal weighting. If the blend improves, keep it; if not, the model lacks sufficient diversity to help.
  - `52200959:e8#3` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Master; steps 52200959:35->36, 52200959:37->38): Ensemble all available model families even if some are individually weaker. A model scoring 0.41 individually can still improve a 0.33 ensemble when blended, because it captures different patterns. Weight by inverse error rather than excluding weak models.
  - `53747598:e3#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Master; steps 53747598:14->15): Add models that vary along multiple axes simultaneously: backbone architecture (efficientnet vs. convnext vs. ViT), input format (kaggle spectrograms vs. self-generated vs. raw EEG images), and inference strategy (TTA, different augmentations). Each new model group should differ from existing ones on at least two of these axes to maximize ensemble diversity.

## 23. standalone_probe_before_ensemble_integration  [L3]  —  6 kernels, 2 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When a new model variant or backbone is available and you want to decide whether to add it to an existing ensemble, or when one ensemble component appears dominant after a blend improvement.
- **Action:** Test the new model's or strong component's predictions in isolation first (disabling all other models) to get its standalone score. If it scores substantially worse than the ensemble (e.g., >2-5% relative), keep the ensemble and instead tune blend weights to increase that component's contribution. If it is competitive, try blending it with the existing ensemble as the next step. Do not iterate on the single-model path if it clearly underperforms the blend.
- **Exceptions:** A weak standalone model can still improve an ensemble through diversity, so rejecting it based solely on standalone performance may be premature (18423958:e6#1 counter_evidence, 52551258:e10#1). Consider testing the blend anyway if the model is architecturally diverse from existing members.
- **Support:** kernels 17616127, 18350823, 18423958, 49524919, 52551258, 52860091; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Contributor': 1, 'Expert': 2, 'Master': 1, 'Grandmaster': 2}; episode reached new best: {'no': 4, 'yes': 2}
- **Cells:** L3/probe/new_idea/part3, L3/probe/new_idea/part4
- **Examples:**
  - `17616127:e24#1` (commonlitreadability, Contributor; steps 17616127:85->86): Submit the new backbone's fold-averaged predictions alone (disabling all other models) as a single probe. If the standalone score is worse than the current best ensemble, do not discard the new backbone—instead fold it back into the blend as an additional component. If it matches or beats the ensemble, consider simplifying to that backbone.
  - `18350823:e7#1` (commonlitreadability, Expert; steps 18350823:15->16): Submit the strong component alone as a one-shot probe. If it regresses substantially (e.g., >2% relative), immediately revert to the blend and instead tune blend weights to increase that component's contribution. Do not iterate on the single-model path.
  - `18423958:e6#1` (commonlitreadability, Master; steps 18423958:13->14): Submit the new backbone as a standalone model first. If it scores substantially worse than the existing ensemble (e.g., >5% relative regression), abandon it as a standalone replacement. Only consider adding it to the blend if its standalone score is competitive with individual components of the current ensemble.
  - `49524919:e34#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 49524919:158->159, 49524919:159->160, 49524919:160->161, 49524919:161->162): Submit each major model group in isolation (disabling all others) to measure its standalone score. If every component scores worse than the blend, the blend is validated. Then re-enable all components — the blend with any checkpoint updates discovered during probing often yields a further improvement. Limit probing to 2-4 submissions to conserve budget.
  - `52551258:e10#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 52551258:18->19): Test the new model in isolation first (commenting out the old model) rather than immediately ensembling it. If it scores worse than the current best standalone model, do not add it to the ensemble—move on to other ideas. This avoids polluting a working ensemble with a weak component.
  - `52860091:e4#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 52860091:13->14): Keep the entire inference and ensembling pipeline identical and change only the model config flag. Submit the single-architecture result first to get its standalone score. If the gain is marginal or comparable, treat the new architecture as an ensemble component rather than a replacement, and next try blending both architectures' predictions.

## 24. multi_fold_prediction_averaging  [L2]  —  5 kernels, 5 comps, 5 items

- **Context:** When multiple K-fold checkpoints are available from cross-validation training and only a single fold's predictions are being used at inference time.
- **Action:** Average predictions across all K fold checkpoints before post-processing (rounding, thresholding, etc.). After switching to multi-fold averaging, re-optimize any downstream post-processing thresholds since the prediction distribution changes. Expect modest but consistent variance reduction gains (typically 0.05-0.5% on classification/regression metrics).
- **Exceptions:** Architecture quality can outweigh fold-averaging gains: a single checkpoint from a stronger architecture may beat a 5-fold ensemble from a weaker one (15082684:e5#1). Also, fold averaging alone won't help if other pipeline issues dominate.
- **Support:** kernels 15082684, 17616127, 49576186, 55621328, 6803050; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Master': 3, 'Contributor': 1, 'Expert': 1}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 2, 'no': 3}

## 32. weight_strongest_model_highest_in_blend  [L2]  —  5 kernels, 3 comps, 7 items

- **Context:** When blending 2-4 models of varying standalone quality (measured by validation or LB scores).
- **Action:** Assign the highest blend weight (≥0.5) to the model with the best standalone performance. Give equal smaller weights to remaining models. Start with a simple ratio (e.g., 0.5/0.25/0.25 for three models) rather than equal weighting. Increase the best model's share in ~0.1 steps up to about 0.5-0.6 but do not exceed 0.6 for a single model in a multi-way blend, as diminishing diversity causes regression. When the quality gap is very large (>10% relative), assign weights roughly proportional to model quality (inversely proportional to error), giving weak models small weights (e.g., 0.1) and strong models large weights (e.g., 0.4+). If the weaker model doesn't improve the blend even at low weight, remove it entirely rather than continuing to tune.
- **Exceptions:** If models are highly correlated, even 0.5 for the strongest may be too high for the weaker ones to contribute meaningfully. When the quality gap is very large (>30%), even a small weight for the weaker model may add noise; test the stronger model alone first (49524919:e15#1).
- **Support:** kernels 18423958, 49524919, 50496431, 53747598, 73671444; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Master': 3, 'Grandmaster': 4}; episode reached new best: {'no': 3, 'yes': 4}

If adding a backbone worsens the score, reduce its weight or remove it rather than discarding the ensemble. Keep the strongest proven model's weight ≥0.5.

## 33. stop_weight_tuning_switch_to_diversity  [L3]  —  5 kernels, 3 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** Blend-weight tuning across existing ensemble members has plateaued (diminishing returns, regressions, or 3-4 failed attempts) and the current set of component models has been fixed for several iterations, with component predictions likely correlated.
- **Action:** Stop tuning blend weights. Instead, invest effort in adding a new, architecturally diverse model component (new architectures, retrieval-based features, more folds) to expand ensemble diversity. If a weak but diverse component is available, blend it at moderate weight (30-40%) first to confirm improvement. ## 34. revert_fully_before_next_experiment_on_regression  [L3]  —  5 kernels, 3 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** When a configuration change (single or compound) causes a clear score regression compared to a known-good baseline.
- **Action:** Fully revert to the last known-good configuration before trying the next change. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. If a partial revert doesn't recover the baseline score, inspect which components are actually running (e.g., missing ensemble members). Only after recovering the baseline, introduce the next candidate change.

## 35. large_pipeline_build_without_intermediate_submissions  [L3]  —  5 kernels, 3 comps, 5 items

## 39. isolate_changes_on_regression  [L3]  —  5 kernels, 2 comps, 6 items

- **Context:** A submission that bundled multiple changes simultaneously (e.g., new checkpoint + new transforms, hyperparameters, features, post-processing, model swap + preprocessing change) caused a score regression, making it impossible to attribute the cause.
- **Action:** Revert the most speculative/auxiliary changes first (e.g., novel post-processing, hyperparameter tweaks) while keeping the primary structural change being tested. Submit the simpler variant to isolate the primary change's effect. If the score still doesn't improve, the primary change itself is the problem; if it does improve, the reverted auxiliary change was harmful. Only after confirming the feature's value, layer on hyperparameter tuning one change at a time. Do not try entirely new combinations on top of the failed bundle.

This is risky when submission budget is limited.

## 42. discretize_predictions_for_rank_based_metrics  [L2]  —  5 kernels, 1 comps, 7 items

- **Context:** The evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation), the model outputs continuous predictions, and the ground truth labels take only a few discrete values (e.g., averages of crowd ratings).
- **Action:** Post-process predictions by snapping/discretizing them to the known discrete target levels. Start conservatively with the most binary/sparse columns (e.g., clamp extremes near 0 or 1). Expand incrementally, one or a few columns at a time, verifying each batch improves the score. If a batch causes regression, revert entirely rather than partially fixing. Check for degeneracy (all values collapsed to one bin) and revert affected columns to continuous predictions.
- **Exceptions:** Scaling/discretizing all columns at once can hurt (7548275 v24, 7823861 v22-v23). Binarizing near-binary columns may not help if the model already captures ranking well (6803050:e13#2). KBinsDiscretizer may be replaced by epsilon-based quantization for more adaptive results (7018718:e13#1).
- **Support:** kernels 6803050, 7018718, 7548275, 7573212, 7823861; comps google-quest-challenge; tiers {'Master': 1, 'Expert': 3, 'Contributor': 1, nan: 2}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 6, 'no': 1}
- **Cells:** L2/postprocessing_rounding_and_thresholding
- **Examples:**
  - `6803050:e14#1` (google-quest-challen, Master; steps 6803050:58->59, 6803050:59->60): Inspect the training label distribution for each target column. For columns with large gaps between discrete levels, apply a threshold that snaps predictions below a cutoff to the nearest discrete level observed in training. Test the exact replacement value (0 vs. the actual discrete level) since Spearman is sensitive to ties. If the gain is marginal after one or two tries, move on.
  - `7018718:e11#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7018718:37->38, 7018718:41->42, 7018718:42->43, 7018718:44->45): After discretizing predictions, check each column for degeneracy (e.g., all values identical). If a column collapsed to a single value, revert it to the original continuous predictions. Then rescale each column to [0,1] via min-max normalization. This preserves ranking information in edge-case columns while still benefiting from discretization elsewhere.
  - `7018718:e13#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7018718:46->47, 7018718:47->48, 7018718:49->50, 7018718:51->52): For each target column, tune an epsilon threshold on CV using a log-spaced grid. At inference, sort predictions, collapse consecutive values closer than epsilon into the same value, then unsort. Guard against collapsing all values to a constant by checking uniqueness before overwriting. Tune coefficients offline on CV, then apply at submission time.
  - `7548275:e6#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7548275:21->22, 7548275:23->24, 7548275:24->25, 7548275:25->26): Start by applying discretization/scaling to columns with the most discrete target distributions (e.g., binary or few-level columns). Test scaling all columns; if it regresses, revert to a curated subset. Expand the subset one or a few columns at a time, using per-column OOF Spearman comparisons to decide which columns benefit. Stop when marginal gains become negligible.
  - `7573212:e5#1` (google-quest-challen, Contributor; steps 7573212:7->8, 7573212:8->9): Bin continuous predictions into evenly-spaced discrete levels using a cut/digitize function. Start with a number of bins roughly matching the number of distinct target levels (e.g., 10-20). Apply this after ensembling (average first, then discretize). Test on validation before submitting.
  - `7823861:e4#1` (google-quest-challen, nan; steps 7823861:15->16, 7823861:16->17): Start with conservative post-processing: only clamp extreme predictions (near 0 or 1) to their boundary values. Submit and verify improvement. Then incrementally add finer-grained binning for intermediate ranges. If a round of expanded rules causes regression, revert the new rules and add them back selectively. Derive thresholds from training label distributions.

## 43. isolate_one_change_per_submission  [L3]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 8 items

- **Context:** When you have multiple candidate changes (e.g., blend weight + model version, preprocessing + checkpoint, discrete configuration options) and limited submission budget.
- **Action:** Change only one lever per submission to enable attribution. If a change regresses, revert it before trying the next option. If a combined change regresses, you cannot tell which component caused it and must spend additional submissions to disentangle. If all options score below baseline after a full sweep, abandon the lever entirely. If you must bundle changes, first test each independently offline/locally. When a regression is so clear that one factor is obviously the culprit, it is acceptable to revert it while simultaneously testing the next option.
- **Exceptions:** 7018718:e4#1 notes the author violated one-at-a-time when the model subset regression was so clear, combining revert with a new test. Acceptable to bundle changes when you have strong offline CV evidence for one component and are using the submission to validate the combination.
- **Support:** kernels 50496431, 60197293, 7018718, 77450317; comps equity-post-hct-survival-pre, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, learning-agency-lab-automate; tiers {'Grandmaster': 5, 'Expert': 3}; episode reached new best: {'no': 7, 'yes': 1}
- **Cells:** L3/sweep/new_idea/part4, L3/sweep/new_idea/part5
- **Examples:**
  - `50496431:e32#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:105->106): Revert one of the changes and resubmit. If the score partially recovers but doesn't match the original best, the other change is also harmful. Never change two independent levers in one submission if you need to attribute the effect; if you already did, revert one at a time to diagnose.
  - `50496431:e41#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:149->150, 50496431:152->153): When a multi-change edit regresses, first restore the ensemble members that were removed (the highest-impact, most reversible change) before investigating other parameters. Re-enable previously-working model predictions to recover baseline performance, then try smaller modifications one at a time.
  - `50496431:e52#1` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50496431:200->201, 50496431:201->202, 50496431:204->205): Try ablating members and switching blending strategy (weighted→mean or vice versa) one change at a time. If the score regresses, immediately restore the removed members and blending method before trying the next variant. Do not stack multiple untested changes (member removal + preprocessing change) in one submission—if you do and regress, revert all changes together.
  - `60197293:e19#2` (learning-agency-lab-, Expert; steps 60197293:131->132, 60197293:132->133): When a parameter change causes a large regression, revert to the previous best value first, then try a smaller step in the same direction. If the smaller step also fails to improve, abandon that direction and accept the original value.
  - `7018718:e4#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7018718:10->11, 7018718:11->12, 7018718:12->13): Change one configuration at a time, submit, and compare to the established baseline. If a change regresses, revert it before trying the next option. If all options score below baseline after a full sweep, abandon the lever and move to a different one (e.g., different model architecture or checkpoint).
  - `7018718:e9#1` (google-quest-challen, Expert; steps 7018718:27->28, 7018718:28->29, 7018718:29->30, 7018718:30->31): After a new best from a combined change, isolate factors by first testing a different checkpoint with preprocessing disabled, then re-enable preprocessing options one at a time. If no combination beats the original, stop after 3-4 attempts and try a different lever entirely. Always submit each variant to get leaderboard signal.

## 44. refactor_then_verify_before_submitting  [L3]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 5 items

- **Context:** When the notebook has grown complex with accumulated code (inline feature engineering, dead code, repetitive blocks) and a major structural refactor is needed to speed iteration.
- **Action:** Refactor in small incremental steps. After each structural change, do a verification run with no other changes to confirm outputs/validation metrics match pre-refactor levels before submitting or tuning further. Bundle housekeeping with a small low-risk improvement (e.g., adding a checkpoint, toggling a model) so the submission also tests a hypothesis rather than being wasted on pure refactoring.
- **Exceptions:** 73937748:e13#1: author never fully recovered pre-episode best, suggesting refactoring can inadvertently change ensemble composition. 7670859:e3#1: no submission was made during refactoring episode, so LB impact was unconfirmed.

- **Cells:** L3/consolidate/new_idea
- **Examples:**

Simultaneously add new model checkpoints (extra seeds/folds) to the ensemble. Submit to verify no regression and confirm the new members help. This bundles housekeeping with a low-risk improvement so the cleanup commit is not wasted.

In the main notebook, read those files directly. After refactoring, do a verification run with no other changes to confirm outputs match before tuning further. Only then adjust training hyperparameters.
  - `27799930:e12#2` (amex-default-predict, Contributor; steps 27799930:73->74, 27799930:74->75): After a large refactor, make one small conservative adjustment (e.g., slightly increase ensemble diversity via folds/seeds), then do a no-change re-run to verify stability. Only submit after confirming validation metrics are at least as good as before the refactor.

First refactor utilities (target transforms, classes), then toggle model groups on/off one family at a time. Accept small score drops (<0.001) as noise from refactoring. If a step causes a larger drop (>0.001), investigate and compensate in the next step rather than reverting. Keep all steps submitted so you have a regression trail.

## 45. sequential_model_load_predict_free_for_ensembles  [L2]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 4 items

- **Context:** When running inference with multiple large models (transformers or vision) sequentially on a GPU with limited memory, such as Kaggle's environment.
- **Action:** Load one model at a time, run predictions, then explicitly delete the model and call gc.collect() (and torch.cuda.empty_cache() for PyTorch). Accumulate predictions in CPU memory and average after all models finish. If OOM persists after deletion, also reduce batch size. Do not hold multiple models in GPU memory simultaneously.
- **Exceptions:** For very small models, simultaneous loading may be fine. In 7823861, the root cause was multi-model loading rather than batch size, so fix memory management before adjusting batch size.
- **Support:** kernels 15164527, 17616127, 50376011, 7823861; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c, ranzcr-clip-catheter-line-cl; tiers {'Expert': 1, 'Contributor': 1, 'Grandmaster': 1, nan: 1}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 3, 'no': 1}
- **Cells:** L2/memory_and_compute_optimization
- **Examples:**
  - `15164527:e1#2` (ranzcr-clip-catheter, Expert; steps 15164527:2->3, 15164527:3->4): First add explicit del and optionally torch.cuda.empty_cache() after each model's inference pass. If OOM persists, halve the batch size. For large image models at 640px, batch size 64 is a safer starting point than 128 on a single GPU.
  - `17616127:e18#2` (commonlitreadability, Contributor; steps 17616127:66->67): Insert gc.collect() (and optionally torch.cuda.empty_cache()) after each batch or after each model's predictions to free memory. If the run still fails, reduce the number of models loaded per session or delete model objects explicitly between loads.
  - `50376011:e2#2` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Grandmaster; steps 50376011:7->8): For each checkpoint: restore config, load weights, run prediction, save outputs, then explicitly free GPU memory (gc.collect + torch.cuda.empty_cache) before loading the next model. Accumulate predictions in CPU memory and average after all models have run. This avoids OOM while enabling arbitrary ensemble sizes.
  - `7823861:e1#2` (google-quest-challen, nan; steps 7823861:2->3, 7823861:3->4): Start with batch_size=1 for large models to minimize memory. If that fails, fix the memory issue (e.g., don't hold multiple models simultaneously) rather than increasing batch size. Only increase batch size after confirming single-model inference works.

## 46. one_change_per_submission  [L2]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 4 items

- **Context:** When testing risky or untested changes and leaderboard submissions are the primary feedback mechanism.
- **Action:** Make only one substantive change per submission so you can attribute gains or regressions to that specific change. If the score regresses, revert before trying the next change. Never combine a new model addition with structural code refactoring and hyperparameter changes in a single submission.
- **Exceptions:** When recovering from a failed experiment, bundling a revert with one promising change can be efficient (50496431:e43#3). Bundling complementary changes sometimes works when changes are low-risk (49576186:e9#1 counter_evidence).

Then layer the ensembling technique on top and submit again. This lets you attribute gains to each change independently and avoids masking a regression in one with a gain in the other. If the first change regresses, revert before trying the second.

When multiple changes are made simultaneously and the score regresses, you cannot identify which change caused the regression and cannot selectively revert. Instead, add one change at a time, submit, and only stack the next change if the previous one was neutral or positive.

If you must bundle changes, ensure you can revert each independently. Never combine a new model addition with structural code refactoring and hyperparameter changes in a single submission.

## 47. revert_multi_change_regression  [L2]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 4 items

- **Context:** A submission regresses significantly after changing multiple variables (hyperparameters, model, preprocessing, etc.) simultaneously, making it impossible to attribute the cause.
- **Action:** Revert entirely to the last known-good configuration rather than attempting incremental fixes. Then re-apply changes one at a time, submitting or validating after each, to isolate which change caused the regression. Do not attempt to salvage the new combination by tweaking within it.
- **Exceptions:** 50496431:e36#3 shows partial reverts (reverting preprocessing but keeping structural additions) can work when some changes are independently valid, though recovery may be incomplete.

Do not spend multiple iterations toggling a minor ensemble member (±0.0002 effect) when the regression is large (−0.009). Instead, bisect: test features alone, then new members alone.
  - `7823861:e5#2` (google-quest-challen, nan; steps 7823861:22->23, 7823861:23->24): When a multi-parameter change causes a large regression, revert entirely to the last known-good version rather than attempting to fix individual parameters. Then re-apply changes one at a time or in small groups, submitting after each, to isolate which change caused the regression. Never change more parameters in one step than you changed in your best-performing step.

Instead, pivot to a qualitatively different change (e.g., enabling a disabled model branch, switching feature generation method) that has higher expected impact. Reserve fine-tuning for after structural decisions are settled.

## 52. switch_from_weight_tuning_to_diversity  [L3]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 4 items

- **Context:** When reweighting a fixed set of ensemble components yields no improvement, or when several consecutive attempts to tune preprocessing/weights fail to beat the current best.
- **Action:** Stop tuning weights and introduce a new diverse component (different model family, architecture, or checkpoint) to increase ensemble diversity. Only resume weight tuning after the new component is validated. Diminishing returns on weight sweeps signal that the current model set's capacity is saturated.
- **Exceptions:** none
- **Support:** kernels 17616127, 27656049, 50496431, 73937748; comps amex-default-prediction, commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Contributor': 1, 'Expert': 1, 'Grandmaster': 1, 'Master': 1}; episode reached new best: {'yes': 3, 'no': 1}
- **Cells:** L3/sweep/new_idea/part4

Only after the new component is validated should you fine-tune weights.

If each HP step yields diminishing or small improvements relative to the gap to top scores, that confirms the feature set is the bottleneck. Resume HP tuning only after the feature set is enriched.

Diminishing returns on parameter sweeps signal that the current model set's capacity is saturated.

Do not iterate further on the same parameters.

## 53. stop_sweep_after_three_failures  [L3]  —  4 kernels, 4 comps, 4 items

- **Context:** When 3+ submitted attempts exploring the same lever (e.g., checkpoint variants, hyperparameter direction, backbone swaps) all fail to beat the current best score.
- **Action:** Stop the sweep on that lever and pivot to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., new model family, different feature set, ensemble blending strategy). Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future ensembles rather than discarding it.
- **Exceptions:** If the leaderboard is extremely noisy (e.g., ~7 evaluation rows as in CommonLit), regressions may be noise rather than true signal, so consider local CV before abandoning.
- **Support:** kernels 17371717, 49576186, 6803050, 77347591; comps commonlitreadabilityprize, equity-post-hct-survival-pre, google-quest-challenge, hms-harmful-brain-activity-c; tiers {'Master': 2, 'Expert': 2}; episode reached new best: {'no': 4}

Resume with a fresh checkpoint trained under the best-identified variant.
  - `49576186:e5#3` (hms-harmful-brain-ac, Expert; steps 49576186:28->29, 49576186:31->32, 49576186:33->34): After three failed submissions exploring the same lever (backbone/LR/sampling), abandon that direction and switch to an orthogonal lever such as data augmentation or preprocessing changes. The signal that the lever is exhausted is that even partial reversions toward the baseline config don't recover the best score.
  - `6803050:e10#2` (google-quest-challen, Master; steps 6803050:41->42, 6803050:47->48, 6803050:48->49): After 3+ submitted attempts that all regress from the baseline along the same lever, stop the sweep and change strategy. Move to a qualitatively different approach such as combining the best configurations via weighted blending rather than continuing to test individual variants. Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future ensembles rather than discarding it.
